content: 1. Observational studies have demonstrated that opioid substitution therapy significantly reduces mortality compared to individuals not receiving care. 2. Among people living with HIV who inject drugs, access to opioid substitution therapy has been associated with improved antiretroviral therapy (ART) outcomes. 3. A systematic review identified one randomized trial and three observational studies evaluating the impact of delivering ART in settings that also provide opioid substitution therapy. 4. Many of these studies had small sample sizes, which limited their statistical power. 5. Some studies observed trends toward improved viral suppression and reduced mortality, while others reported similar rates of viral suppression and mortality. 6. The recommendation emphasizes expanding access to ART by integrating its delivery into settings that provide opioid substitution therapy. 7. Coverage of opioid substitution therapy remains low in many regions, and policymakers should assess the feasibility of offering this therapy in conjunction with HIV care and treatment services. 8. In settings where health authorities do not manage drug-dependence services, HIV programs must collaborate closely with social welfare departments, community organizations, and non-governmental organizations to ensure service provision. 9. Decentralizing ART initiation and maintenance to peripheral health facilities is strongly recommended, despite the low quality of evidence supporting this approach. 10. Initiating ART at peripheral health facilities and maintaining it at the community level, such as through outreach sites, health posts, or community-based organizations, is also strongly recommended, with moderate-quality evidence. 11. Decentralizing HIV care to primary care settings can alleviate the burden on hospitals, improve equity by increasing access in rural areas, and reduce transportation costs, which are significant barriers to care. 12. In high HIV-burden settings, decentralization can reduce long hospital wait times and bring services closer to patients' homes, improving retention in care. 13. Community-based interventions play a critical role in providing HIV testing, care, treatment, and social support, and decentralization can strengthen community engagement and optimize service access. 14. Systematic reviews have shown that decentralizing ART initiation and maintenance to peripheral health facilities reduces patient attrition, primarily by decreasing losses to follow-up. 15. Community-based maintenance of ART has shown comparable rates of attrition to centralized care after 12 months. 16. Program managers should consider the number of people living with HIV likely to use decentralized services, whether decentralization reduces travel distances for patients, and whether it alleviates workloads at centralized facilities. 17. Effective decentralization requires links to diagnostic and medicine supply chains, health worker training, and supervision to maintain care quality. 18. Task shifting, which redistributes clinical tasks from highly qualified health workers to those with shorter training, is essential to address workforce shortages in high HIV-burden settings. 19. Trained non-physician clinicians, midwives, and nurses can initiate and maintain first-line ART, and community health workers can dispense ART between clinical visits, with strong recommendations supported by moderate-quality evidence. 20. Task shifting improves ART access in rural and underserved areas and allows physicians to focus on managing complex cases, such as co-infections and treatment failures. 21. WHO guidelines recommend that nurses and non-physician clinicians initiate and maintain ART and that community health workers monitor patients during long-term follow-up. 22. Evidence shows no difference in mortality or care retention when ART is managed by nurses, non-physician clinicians, or community health workers compared to physicians, provided adequate training, supervision, and referral systems are in place. 23. Patient education is crucial to dispel misconceptions that care provided by non-physician health workers is of lower quality than that provided by physicians. 24. Strengthening laboratory and diagnostic services is critical to ensure accurate and reliable testing, with a focus on leadership, governance, and quality assurance systems. 25. Expanding access to HIV viral load testing requires strengthening laboratory infrastructure, leveraging existing networks, and ensuring high-quality diagnostics. 26. Strategic planning is necessary to harmonize testing platforms, validate diagnostic algorithms, and ensure cost-effectiveness in laboratory services. 27. Dedicated specimen referral systems must be strengthened to ensure timely and reliable transport of samples and rapid reporting of test results to improve patient care. 28. Increasing access to viral load testing involves phased expansion of monitoring services to peripheral facilities and leveraging existing diagnostic networks. 29. Training and certifying health workers to perform diagnostic testing and ensuring quality assurance are essential for effective implementation. 30. Countries should consider long-term reforms to support task shifting and introduce new health worker roles, such as peer counselors, within a nationally endorsed regulatory framework.
